title: "PocketSolver"
subtitle: "Learning to score poker decisions"
author: "[Ryan Zheng]{.member-name}, [Amy Sun]{.member-name}, [Rain Piao]{.member-name}, [Connier Wu]{.member-name}, [Aaron Lee]{.member-name}, [Nicholas Park]{.member-name}, [Maksim Fu]{.member-name}, [Sam Jiang]{.member-name}, [Emily Du]{.member-name}, [Justin Zhang]{.member-name}, [Alexander An]{.member-name}, [Sumedh Kamat]{.member-name}, [Jerry Huang]{.member-name}"
date: "2026-11-13"
date-format: "MMMM D, YYYY"
description: "A structured poker decision model, scenario-grouped evaluation, and experiments with opponent history."
abstract: |
  Poker decisions combine visible cards, betting history, hidden information,
  and a changing menu of possible actions. We study a compact alternative to
  generating an answer: jointly encode the situation and its candidate actions,
  then score each action with a shared prediction head. We compare four
  pretrained encoders and two heads on a 10,000-example PokerBench development
  pool using five scenario-grouped folds. ModernBERT with a linear head has the
  highest observed exact-action agreement, while all eight transformer variants
  improve log loss over a linear candidate baseline. We also investigate causal
  opponent-history summaries in controlled Leduc forecasting and observed-action
  prediction from real Hold'em histories. History improves the controlled
  forecasting task, but the current summaries do not establish a benefit for
  the Hold'em transformer. PocketSolver makes the decision model available in
  an interactive demonstration. These experiments measure reference or observed
  action agreement; they do not establish profitable or unexploitable play.
---

# Poker as a structured decision problem

A poker hand asks a deceptively compact question: **What should Hero do?** The
answer depends on the visible cards, position, pot, previous actions, and the
available choices. Calling and folding are distinct actions; betting 28 big blinds
and betting 51 big blinds are also distinct actions. A model that chooses the right
action type can still miss the reference by choosing a different amount.

Our starting point is to make those choices explicit. Rather than ask a language
model to write an answer and parse it back into an action, we supply the candidate
actions alongside the situation. The model returns one score for each candidate.
This preserves the exact supplied sizes and supports menus of different lengths.

@fig-hand shows a recorded decision and the scores assigned by the deployed BERT
Mini model. The online explorer includes a postflop success, a preflop success,
and an action-type mistake. They were selected to illustrate behavior, rather
than estimate performance. Each example was held out by this specific checkpoint.

::: {#fig-hand}

<img class="static-fallback" src="generated/figures/hand.svg" alt="A held-out postflop decision, its candidate actions, BERT Mini probabilities, and the reference action.">
</div>
:::

![](generated/figures/hand.pdf)

on request and is excluded from model inputs.

The project separates three questions. First, can a structured encoder learn to
agree with PokerBench reference actions? Second, can previous behavior help predict
an opponent's next action? Third, does appending those histories improve a
transformer on real Hold'em decisions? These questions use different targets and
data, so their scores should be interpreted within each experiment.

# Scoring actions in one forward pass

## Joint encoding and a shared head

The input is a context string and an ordered list of candidate actions. The encoder
adapter adds the fixed question, "What should Hero do?" We serialize the state,
question, and all candidates into one sequence with separator tokens. A pretrained
encoder produces contextual representations for every token. For each candidate,
we average the representations of its own tokens and apply the same scoring head.

For candidate $a_i$ with token positions $S_i$, the model computes

$$
h_i = \frac{1}{|S_i|}\sum_{t\in S_i} H_t, \qquad
z_i = g_\theta(h_i), \qquad
p(a_i\mid x,A) = \frac{\exp z_i}{\sum_{j\in A}\exp z_j}.
$$

Here $H$ is the encoder output for the joint sequence and $A$ is the supplied menu.
The head $g_\theta$ is either a linear projection or a two-layer MLP with a ReLU
activation. Training updates both the encoder and head using cross-entropy on the
reference candidate index. Candidate padding is masked before normalization.

::: {#fig-architecture}
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
<div data-widget="architecture" class="interactive-figure">
<img class="static-fallback" src="generated/figures/architecture.svg" alt="State, question and all candidates pass through one encoder, candidate pooling, and a shared scoring head.">
</div>
:::
::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
![](generated/figures/architecture.pdf)
:::

All options share one encoder pass and one scoring head. Candidate representations
can attend to the context and to other candidates. The web illustration highlights
whole action spans schematically; it does not display exact tokenizer boundaries
or measured attention weights.
:::

The design reuses pretrained language representations in the spirit of encoder
fine-tuning [@bert]. It avoids generating an action token by token, but a single
forward pass is not itself a measured speed advantage. Sequence length, model
size, hardware, batching, and serving overhead all affect latency.

## What the interface guarantees

The input boundary keeps labels and source identifiers separate from context and
candidates. Contexts contain only cards already dealt and permitted visible
information. We do not invent missing stacks or opponent profiles. Inputs that
exceed the configured token limit fail explicitly rather than silently losing
state or candidate tokens.

One limitation follows from joint encoding: candidate order is visible through
positional encodings. Sharing a head does not make the model permutation invariant.
Candidate-order augmentation and explicit order-robustness evaluation remain
natural follow-up experiments. The model can choose only among the supplied
candidates; it does not establish that those candidates exhaust legal or useful
poker actions.

# Evaluating beyond repeated scenarios

## Sources and splits

Our primary action-choice experiment uses the pinned PokerBench training sources
[@pokerbench]. The source audit validates 63,200 preflop rows and 500,000 postflop
rows. The development working pool samples 5,000 examples from each source, giving
10,000 examples in total. This sampling balance describes the experiment; it is
not an estimate of the frequency of these situations in play.

An early walkthrough used a context-grouped 8,000/2,000 split. Identical contexts
never crossed that boundary, but related scenarios often did: 91.8% of validation
rows had a scenario group represented in training. We therefore use a broader,
answer-free scenario grouping for the model comparison reported here.

Preflop groups use the full previous betting history. Postflop groups use the
sorted ranks of the first three board cards, keeping suit variants and later
streets together. Across the five maintained folds, neither specified scenario
groups nor exact contexts overlap between training and held-out examples. Every
example receives exactly one held-out prediction per model. This grouping is a
specific stress test; it cannot establish independence under every possible
notion of poker similarity.

::: {#tbl-folds}
| Fold | Training examples | Held-out examples | Shared scenario groups |
| --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 1 | 8,070 | 1,930 | 0 |
| 2 | 7,889 | 2,111 | 0 |
| 3 | 8,067 | 1,933 | 0 |
| 4 | 7,911 | 2,089 | 0 |
| 5 | 8,063 | 1,937 | 0 |

Five fixed development folds. Groups are defined without reference labels.
:::

## Baselines, training, and metrics

We compare uniform candidate probabilities, a training-only option prior, and a
linear candidate model with four pretrained encoders: BERT Mini, MiniLM,
DistilBERT, and ModernBERT. Each encoder receives both a linear head and an MLP
head, for eight transformer configurations and 40 fitted folds.

Every transformer fit uses seed 42, three fixed epochs, batch size 16, encoder
learning rate $2\times10^{-5}$, head learning rate $10^{-3}$, weight decay 0.01,
and maximum sequence length 512. The MLP width is 64. Each fold starts with a fresh
encoder, head, and optimizer. Held-out folds do not choose epochs. Baselines are
refitted using each fold's training examples.

**Exact accuracy** measures agreement with the supplied reference candidate,
including its amount. **Log loss** measures the probability assigned to that
reference and penalizes confident mistakes. We also record action-type macro-F1,
Brier score, street-specific performance, and multi-option accuracy. The latter
excludes decisions with only one candidate, which require no choice; such rows
make up 4.64% of the pool. Uniform probabilities have ties, so deterministic
exact accuracy and tie-expected accuracy can differ.

These are development comparisons on an inspected pool, with one training seed.
Selecting a model from this matrix and quoting the same score does not provide
an independent final performance estimate. The maintained workflows do not load
the official test, but some original team submissions had already inspected it.
An independent evaluation needs a predeclared new holdout or nested selection.

# What do the models learn?

## Better probability quality, modest accuracy gains

ModernBERT with a linear head has the highest observed exact accuracy,
[71.92%]{.result key="best_accuracy"}, and the lowest log loss,
[0.6078]{.result key="best_loss"}. The linear candidate baseline reaches
[69.69%]{.result key="baseline_accuracy"} accuracy and
[1.0025]{.result key="baseline_loss"} log loss. The observed accuracy improvement
is [2.23]{.result key="accuracy_gain"} percentage points.

::: {#fig-models}
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
<div data-widget="models" class="interactive-figure">
<img class="static-fallback" src="generated/figures/models.svg" alt="Exact accuracy and log loss for three baselines and eight encoder-head combinations on the same development pool.">
</div>
:::
::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
![](generated/figures/models.pdf)
:::

Development comparison on 10,000 examples, with one held-out prediction per model
and example. Circles denote linear heads and diamonds MLP heads for transformers.
Higher accuracy and lower log loss are better. The web control changes only the
accuracy panel to exclude single-option rows; log loss remains over all examples.
No plotted uncertainty bars are implied by these point estimates.
:::

DistilBERT linear reaches [71.78%]{.result key="distil_accuracy"}, only 14 decisions
behind ModernBERT out of 10,000. That small gap does not establish a reliable
advantage for ModernBERT. Adding an MLP does not consistently improve either
metric across encoders. BERT Mini and MiniLM do not beat the linear candidate
baseline on exact accuracy in these runs, although all eight transformer
configurations have lower log loss.

This distinction matters. A model can make a similar number of top-choice mistakes
while distributing its remaining probability more usefully. Lower log loss is
evidence about reference-label probability quality. It does not establish that
the softmax is calibrated or that it recovers an optimal mixed strategy.

The saved paired scenario-group bootstrap interval for ModernBERT linear's accuracy
gain over the linear candidate baseline is approximately +1.01 to +3.33 percentage
points. That interval conditions on the saved fitted models and specified groups;
it excludes variation from retraining and cannot remove the consequences of
selecting a model after inspecting development results.

## Street-level behavior and illustrative mistakes

An overall average conceals substantial variation between streets. @fig-streets
compares the deployed BERT Mini architecture and ModernBERT, using linear heads.
Preflop agreement is higher than postflop agreement in these runs. Street counts
are uneven: there are 5,000 preflop, 310 flop, 2,021 turn, and 2,669 river decisions.
We should avoid attributing those differences to a single mechanism without
controlled experiments on the representation, menus, and source distributions.

# Does opponent history help?

## Controlled forecasting in Leduc

The first history experiment isolates opponent-action forecasting in a small,
controlled game. We generate Leduc sessions with five policy profiles: tight,
passive, aggressive, balanced, and switching. Fifty opponent instances play two
sessions each, giving 6,000 hands and 12,711 recorded decisions. Repeated sessions
from one opponent stay in the same split.

Predictors receive the observer's own private rank, public board, pot and
contributions, legal menu, and current public action prefix. Opponent private
cards and generator metadata are excluded. History summaries use completed
previous hands and match the relevant action opportunities. They cannot look
at future hands or the current target.

::: {#fig-leduc}
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

<img src="generated/figures/leduc.svg" alt="Controlled Leduc opponent-action forecasting on 2,506 held-out decisions from 10 opponents. History windows are counts of completed hands. The 64-hand primary window was selected using validation log loss; the plotted test points are descriptive comparisons within this one simulated population.">
</picture>
</div>
:::
::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
![](generated/figures/leduc.pdf)
:::

Controlled Leduc opponent-action forecasting on 2,506 held-out decisions from 10 opponents. History windows are counts of completed hands. The 64-hand primary window was selected using validation log loss; the plotted test points are descriptive comparisons within this one simulated population.
:::

The masked logistic forecaster improves from [59.26%]{.result key="leduc_no_history_accuracy"} to [69.87%]{.result key="leduc_history_selected_accuracy"} accuracy when given
the selected history summary, while log loss falls from [0.7741]{.result key="leduc_no_history_loss"} to [0.6373]{.result key="leduc_history_selected_loss"}. The
paired whole-opponent bootstrap accuracy interval is +3.42 to +18.97 percentage
points, conditional on the fitted models and generated population.

More history is not uniformly better. All-history summaries are slightly worse
than the selected 64-hand window, and history-based models can lag after a policy
switch. The first-five-hands-after-switch slice contains only 40 decisions from
two opponent instances, so it is descriptive. These results motivate studying
memory under behavior changes; they do not establish human tilt detection or
better Hero decisions.

## Connecting histories to real Hold'em inputs

We next reuse causal summaries with replayed Hold'em histories from the Pluribus
setting [@pluribus]. The target here is the observed human action. This differs
from PokerBench reference-action imitation and from the simulated Leduc task.
The transformer receives a summary of completed-hand opponent behavior appended
to its input. Learned forecaster probabilities are not injected into the model.

The follow-up uses nested training samples of 128, 1,024, and 4,096 decisions and
the same 1,024 validation decisions. The numeric-session-group split, initialization,
seed, learning rates, and one-epoch budget remain fixed. Validation does not
select an epoch or hyperparameter. The public-state forecaster and BERT Mini have
different information boundaries, so their panels are separate matched ablations.

::: {#fig-holdem}
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
<div data-widget="holdem" class="interactive-figure">
<picture class="static-fallback">
<source media="(max-width: 640px)" srcset="generated/figures/holdem-mobile.svg">
<img src="generated/figures/holdem.svg" alt="History ablations across nested training sizes on the same 1,024 Hold&#x27;em validation decisions. The top row shows BERT Mini observed-action prediction; the bottom row shows the public-state forecaster. Each matched pair varies history availability. One epoch on a larger sample entails more optimizer steps, so this is not an equal-compute comparison.">
</picture>
</div>
:::
::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
![](generated/figures/holdem.pdf)
:::

History ablations across nested training sizes on the same 1,024 Hold'em validation decisions. The top row shows BERT Mini observed-action prediction; the bottom row shows the public-state forecaster. Each matched pair varies history availability. One epoch on a larger sample entails more optimizer steps, so this is not an equal-compute comparison.
:::

More training substantially improves prediction, but the appended summaries do
not establish a transformer benefit. At 4,096 training decisions, accuracy is
[73.14%]{.result key="holdem_decision_without_history_accuracy"} without history and [72.46%]{.result key="holdem_decision_with_history_accuracy"} with history. Log loss rises from [0.621108]{.result key="holdem_decision_without_history_loss"} to
[0.651398]{.result key="holdem_decision_with_history_loss"}. The paired session-cluster interval for the accuracy change is -2.51 to
+1.04 percentage points. The apparent history gain in the original 64-example
integration check does not persist in the larger comparison.

The public-state forecaster shows a smaller, different result. At 4,096 training
decisions, history increases accuracy from [68.07%]{.result key="holdem_forecaster_without_history_accuracy"} to [69.34%]{.result key="holdem_forecaster_with_history_accuracy"} and reduces log loss
from [0.705272]{.result key="holdem_forecaster_without_history_loss"} to [0.700675]{.result key="holdem_forecaster_with_history_loss"}. Its paired log-loss interval is -0.008054 to -0.001070.
This supports a modest conditional forecasting benefit, while leaving the
transformer integration question open.

These experiments use one seed, an inspected validation set, and recurring human
aliases across different sessions. Session-cluster intervals do not capture
retraining variation or generalization to unseen players. A useful next experiment
would vary summary representation and memory while preserving paired memberships,
then evaluate a predeclared configuration on new sessions or players.

# Explore PocketSolver

PocketSolver restores the trained BERT Mini encoder and linear candidate head on
CPU. Its 256-hand sample consists of multi-option decisions held out by that
checkpoint. The reference appears after prediction and is excluded from both
model and live LLM inputs. The small checkpoint is a serving choice; it is not
the highest-scoring model in the development matrix.

The live comparison is an illustration, not a controlled model-versus-LLM study.
Provider failures and allowance limits remain visible. A few hands or one browser
timing cannot establish general quality or latency advantages. A proper serving
comparison should record hardware, cold and warm execution, input lengths,
provider settings, successful-response coverage, and repeated measurements.

# Limitations and next steps

The strongest supported conclusion is narrow: jointly encoding a situation and
its candidate actions is a workable supervised interface, and the larger encoders
improve reference-label probability quality with modest accuracy gains over a
strong simple baseline. Causal opponent summaries help in one controlled
forecasting setting, while their current Hold'em transformer integration does
not show a reliable gain.

Several limitations determine what to do next. Independent final evaluation and
multiple training seeds would clarify how much of the observed ranking persists.
Candidate-order perturbations and representation ablations would test whether
models depend on incidental serialization or menu shortcuts. Calibration should
be fitted and assessed on data separate from final evaluation. Controlled serving
measurements would test the practical benefit of avoiding autoregressive output.

Finally, agreement with one reference action is not a payoff evaluation. A single
label does not describe a full solver strategy, and observed human actions need
not be optimal. Claims about profitable, robust, or unexploitable play require
additional repeated-play or game-theoretic evaluation. The present article and
demo provide a reproducible foundation for those experiments.

# Reproducibility and complete results {.appendix}

All reported comparisons use saved protocols and reviewed aggregate results. The
report build validates the main CSV against the corresponding JSON, checks the
demo hand checksum, and joins examples to the saved fold-specific predictions.
It exports the same figures as SVG for the web and vector PDF for LaTeX, together
with source and output hashes. No training or live inference runs while rendering
the article.

The manuscript, bibliography, shared values, and figure identifiers are common
to HTML, PDF, and LaTeX. The print hand and model figures match the default web
states. Web-only controls supplement the paper's argument without carrying claims
that are absent from the static version.
